title: Tower of ivory, house of gold
hookLine: poetic titles from scripture and old hymns

lines: AN IVORY TOWER, USUALLY A PUT-DOWN.
HERE, A NAME FOR A MOTHER.
cards: In everyday English, an ivory tower is usually a put-down. Say someone lives in one, and you mean they're out of touch. But halfway down the Litany of Loreto, the phrase turns up as a name for a mother.
Tower of ivory. House of gold. Then ark of the covenant, gate of heaven, morning star.
They're pictures, set side by side, the way someone who loves a person keeps reaching past ordinary words for a better one. Where do they come from, and why pray in them?

teach.h: A LINE FROM A LOVE SONG.
teach.b: Start with the tower. It comes out of a love song. In the Canticle of Canticles, the Song of Songs, a lover praises the beloved line by line, and in the Douay-Rheims one line reads: "Thy neck as a tower of ivory."

Some Jewish and Christian readers have heard this poem as being about more than two lovers: God and his people, Christ and the Church, God and the soul. Some Christian writers took its lines and gave them to Mary.
It's borrowed love poetry. Ivory is rare, pale and smooth; a tower is strong and stands guard.
Together they make something lovely and sturdy at once, a beauty that doesn't break. Then the house of gold.
In the Book of Kings, Solomon's Temple is covered inside with gold, and in Exodus the ark of the covenant is overlaid with gold, inside and out.

teach.h: A CHILD'S LANGUAGE, NOT A DEFINITION.
teach.b: In those stories the gold isn't for show. It marks the place where God chose to dwell. Catholics call Mary a house of gold for the same reason: she carried Christ.
The house is precious because of who lives in it.

teach.h: THY NECK AS A TOWER OF IVORY.
teach.b: Notice what that does: each title points past her, to the one she held. Catholic teaching about Mary has its careful, exact statements; this stretch began with four of them.
The litany speaks another language, the one a child uses about a mother: not a definition, but a pile of names that never quite says enough.

how: Catholics pray the Litany of Loreto, with titles like Tower of Ivory and House of Gold, in parishes and at home, often after the rosary, answering each title with "pray for us."

o: a scholar who lives out of touch with life
the tallest tower of Solomon's Temple
a title for Mary: lovely and strong at once

games.q: tower of ivory, house of gold — tap the pairs.
p: a line from the Song of Songs
the litany's answer to each name

s: the litany explains each title as it goes
it says the name and answers pray for us. the picture is left for you to sit with.
tower of ivory echoes a love song in scripture
the Canticle of Canticles 7:4: "thy neck as a tower of ivory."
house of gold is about Mary being rich
the gold is the Temple's gold, marking where God dwells. she is called a house of gold because she carried Christ.

games.q: you're adding a line to a litany for a mother. what kind of line do you reach for?
o: a picture borrowed from a love poem.
games.why: the litany reaches for pictures: tower of ivory from the Song of Songs, house of gold from the Temple. it speaks the way a child speaks about a mother.

practice: Let a few of the litany's names go by, one per breath: Mystical rose, Tower of David, Tower of ivory, House of gold, Ark of the covenant, Gate of heaven, Morning star.

Notice the one that makes you stop, and hold its picture a while, a white tower, a golden room, a star before dawn. If you pray, say that one title with its answer, pray for us; if you don't, let the picture be enough.

wordCard.voice: Tower of ivory. A title of Mary from the Litany of Loreto, borrowed from the Song of Songs: beauty and strength in one picture, with its partner, house of gold.

orig.note: Latin: tower of ivory, as the litany says it. house of gold is domus aurea.

carryVoice: Your line: poetry for a mother. Pictures, not definitions, for someone loved. See you at the next title.
